notes.definition: A fuel cell is supplied by an external source of fuel (for example hydrogen) and oxygen or air. The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the fuel cell to produce a potential difference.
explanation: Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel, such as hydrogen, and oxygen or air. Inside the cell the fuel is oxidised electrochemically: instead of burning, it reacts at electrodes so that electrons flow through an external circuit. This produces a potential difference (voltage). Unlike an ordinary cell, a fuel cell does not run flat while fuel and oxygen are still being supplied, so it can produce electricity continuously.

In a hydrogen fuel cell the overall reaction is the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O. This is the same overall reaction as burning hydrogen, but the energy is transferred as electricity rather than mainly by heating. The only product is water, so no carbon dioxide or other pollutants are produced when the fuel cell is used.

Hydrogen is fed to the negative electrode and oxygen (from the air) to the positive electrode, with an electrolyte between them. Electrons released at the negative electrode travel through the external circuit, for example through a motor, to the positive electrode. Hydrogen ions (H⁺) move through the electrolyte to the positive electrode, where they combine with oxygen and electrons to form water.

Hydrogen fuel cells offer a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries, for example in vehicles. Advantages of fuel cells include: water is the only product; they are refuelled quickly rather than recharged over hours; they keep working as long as fuel is supplied; and they do not contain as many toxic metal compounds to dispose of. Disadvantages include: hydrogen is a flammable gas that is difficult to store and needs high-pressure tanks; there are few hydrogen filling stations; fuel cells are expensive; and most hydrogen is made from fossil fuels such as natural gas or by electrolysis using electricity that may come from fossil fuels.

Rechargeable batteries are already widely used, can be charged from the mains at home and need no gas storage. However, they take time to recharge, can only be recharged a limited number of times, store less energy for their mass, and contain metal compounds that must be disposed of or recycled carefully. In an evaluation you should weigh up both sides and come to a justified conclusion.

Higher tier students must write the half equations for the electrode reactions. At the negative electrode hydrogen is oxidised (loses electrons): 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. At the positive electrode oxygen is reduced (gains electrons): O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. Adding the two half equations and cancelling the 4H⁺ and 4e⁻ gives the overall equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
keyFacts: A fuel cell is supplied by an external source of fuel (e.g. hydrogen) and oxygen or air.
The fuel is oxidised electrochemically to produce a potential difference.
Overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
The only product of a hydrogen fuel cell is water.
A fuel cell keeps producing electricity as long as fuel and oxygen are supplied.
Hydrogen fuel cells are a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries.
Hydrogen is flammable and difficult to store; it is often made from fossil fuels.

keyTerms.definition: A cell supplied by an external source of fuel and oxygen or air, in which the fuel is oxidised electrochemically to produce a potential difference.
A fuel cell in which hydrogen is oxidised to water, producing electricity.
Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen); hydrogen is oxidised at the negative electrode of a fuel cell.
Gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen); oxygen is reduced at the positive electrode of a fuel cell.
An equation showing the reaction at one electrode, including the electrons gained or lost.
The voltage produced by a cell, which drives a current through the external circuit.

equations.name: Overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell

workedExamples.title: Combining half equations (Higher)
workedExamples.question: Show how the two half equations in a hydrogen fuel cell combine to give the overall equation.
steps: Cancel 4H⁺ and 4e⁻, which appear on both sides.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating a fuel cell bus
workedExamples.question: A city plans to replace diesel buses with hydrogen fuel cell buses. Give one advantage and one disadvantage, and explain each.
steps: Advantage: the only product is water, so the buses produce no carbon dioxide or harmful gases in the city streets.
Disadvantage: hydrogen is a flammable gas that must be stored in high-pressure tanks, and is often made from natural gas, which releases carbon dioxide.
workedExamples.answer: Cleaner air in the city, but hydrogen is hard to store and may not be produced in a low-carbon way.

workedExamples.title: Identifying oxidation and reduction (Higher)
workedExamples.question: In the half equation 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, is hydrogen oxidised or reduced?
steps: The electrons are on the right-hand side, so they are lost.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a fuel cell burns hydrogen.
misconceptions.right: In fact the hydrogen is oxidised electrochemically at an electrode; there is no flame, and the energy is transferred as electricity.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a fuel cell needs recharging like a battery.
misconceptions.right: In fact a fuel cell is refuelled with hydrogen and keeps working as long as fuel and oxygen are supplied.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think hydrogen fuel cells cause no pollution at all.
misconceptions.right: In fact the cell only produces water, but making, compressing and transporting hydrogen often uses fossil fuels.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often put the electrons on the wrong side of the hydrogen half equation.
misconceptions.right: In fact hydrogen loses electrons, so they appear on the right: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.

realWorld: Some buses, trains and cars run on hydrogen fuel cells, producing only water vapour from their exhausts.
Fuel cells were used on spacecraft to provide electricity, and the water produced was used by astronauts.
Fuel cells can provide back-up electricity for buildings such as hospitals and phone masts.
higherTier: Write the half equations for the electrode reactions in the hydrogen fuel cell.
Add the half equations and cancel H⁺ and e⁻ to get 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Chemistry (8462) only, not Combined Science.
Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel and oxygen or air; the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell is the oxidation of hydrogen to water.
Evaluate the use of hydrogen fuel cells in comparison with rechargeable cells and batteries.
examTips: Say the fuel is 'oxidised electrochemically', not 'burned'.
When evaluating, give advantages and disadvantages of both fuel cells and rechargeable batteries, then a justified conclusion.
Do not claim fuel cells are completely pollution free: mention how the hydrogen is produced.
In half equations, check that atoms and charges balance on both sides.
Remember: oxidation at the negative electrode (hydrogen), reduction at the positive electrode (oxygen).
summary: Fuel cells use an external supply of fuel and oxygen or air.
The fuel is oxidised electrochemically to produce a potential difference.
Hydrogen fuel cell: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O; water is the only product.
Fuel cells are an alternative to rechargeable batteries, with advantages and disadvantages.

questions.question: Which substances are supplied to a hydrogen fuel cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen and oxygen
questions.explanation: A hydrogen fuel cell needs a supply of hydrogen (the fuel) and oxygen, usually from air. Water is the product.

questions.question: What is the only product of the reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: water
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is oxidised to water. There is no carbon in the reactants, so no carbon dioxide forms.

questions.question: In a fuel cell, the fuel is oxidised electrochemically. What does this produce?
markScheme: 1 mark: a potential difference
questions.explanation: The electrochemical oxidation of the fuel causes electrons to flow through the external circuit, producing a potential difference (voltage).

questions.question: In a hydrogen fuel cell, which gas is supplied to the positive electrode?
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen
questions.explanation: Hydrogen goes to the negative electrode and oxygen (or air) to the positive electrode.

questions.question: Which is the balanced equation for the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
questions.explanation: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O is unbalanced (oxygen atoms). 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ is the reverse reaction (electrolysis of water).

questions.question: Why does a hydrogen fuel cell not need recharging?
options: It contains a very large amount of electrolyte
Its reactions are reversed by the motor
It keeps producing electricity as long as fuel and oxygen are supplied
markScheme: 1 mark: works as long as fuel and oxygen are supplied
questions.explanation: The reactants are supplied from outside the cell, so the cell keeps working while hydrogen and oxygen keep flowing in. It is refuelled, not recharged.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of using hydrogen fuel cells in cars?
options: Hydrogen is a flammable gas that is difficult to store
The cars produce carbon dioxide from the exhaust
The fuel cell must be recharged for several hours
Fuel cells only work in pure oxygen
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen is flammable and difficult to store
questions.explanation: Hydrogen must be stored safely in high-pressure tanks. Fuel cell cars do not emit carbon dioxide, are refuelled quickly and can use oxygen from the air.

questions.question: Why might a hydrogen fuel cell car still be responsible for some carbon dioxide emissions?
options: The fuel cell releases carbon dioxide
Water vapour turns into carbon dioxide
Hydrogen is often made from natural gas (a fossil fuel)
Oxygen from the air contains carbon
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen is often made from fossil fuels
questions.explanation: The fuel cell only produces water, but producing hydrogen from natural gas, or by electrolysis using electricity from fossil fuels, releases carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which is an advantage of rechargeable batteries compared with hydrogen fuel cells for cars?
options: They can be refuelled in a few minutes
They can be charged from mains electricity without storing a flammable gas
markScheme: 1 mark: charged from mains without storing a flammable gas
questions.explanation: Rechargeable batteries can be charged at home and need no hydrogen tanks. However, they take longer to recharge and can only be recharged a limited number of times.

questions.question: How does a hydrogen fuel cell differ from burning hydrogen in air?
options: The fuel cell transfers energy mainly as electricity rather than by heating
The fuel cell produces hydrogen peroxide
markScheme: 1 mark: the fuel cell transfers energy as electricity
questions.explanation: Both have the same overall reaction and both produce water, but in a fuel cell the hydrogen is oxidised electrochemically, so energy is transferred as electricity.

questions.question: Which half equation shows the reaction at the negative electrode of a hydrogen fuel cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
questions.explanation: At the negative electrode hydrogen loses electrons (oxidation), so the electrons are on the right. The oxygen equation happens at the positive electrode. 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂ is reduction, the reverse reaction.

questions.question: What type of reaction happens to oxygen at the positive electrode of a hydrogen fuel cell?
options: Neutralisation, because H⁺ ions are used up
markScheme: 1 mark: reduction, oxygen gains electrons
questions.explanation: In O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O the electrons are on the left, so oxygen gains electrons. Gain of electrons is reduction.

questions.question: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, how do H⁺ ions move?
options: Through the electrolyte from the negative electrode to the positive electrode
Through the wire from the positive electrode to the negative electrode
Through the electrolyte from the positive electrode to the negative electrode
They do not move; only electrons move
markScheme: 1 mark: through the electrolyte from negative to positive electrode
questions.explanation: H⁺ ions are made at the negative electrode and used up at the positive electrode, so they move through the electrolyte towards the positive electrode. Electrons, not ions, travel through the wire.

questions.question: Name the two substances that must be supplied to a hydrogen fuel cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen
1 mark: oxygen / air
questions.explanation: The fuel is hydrogen and it reacts with oxygen, which can come from the air.

questions.question: Name the product formed in a hydrogen fuel cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: water
questions.explanation: The overall reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

questions.question: Describe what is meant by a fuel cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: a cell supplied by an external source of fuel and oxygen or air
1 mark: in which the fuel is oxidised electrochemically to produce a potential difference / electricity
questions.explanation: The two key ideas are the external supply of fuel and oxygen, and the electrochemical oxidation that produces a voltage.

questions.question: Hydrogen fuel cell buses are described as 'zero emission at the point of use'. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the only product is water, so no carbon dioxide or other pollutants are released by the bus
questions.explanation: The bus itself only releases water vapour. 'At the point of use' means emissions from producing the hydrogen are not counted.

questions.question: Write a word equation and a balanced symbol equation for the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen + oxygen → water
1 mark: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
questions.explanation: Two hydrogen molecules react with one oxygen molecule to make two water molecules, so the numbers of atoms balance.

questions.question: Give two advantages of using hydrogen fuel cells rather than rechargeable batteries to power a car.
acceptedAnswers: work as long as fuel supplied
fewer toxic chemicals to dispose of
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: only product is water; refuelled quickly instead of recharging for hours; keep working while fuel supplied / longer range; fewer toxic metal compounds to dispose of; batteries can only be recharged a limited number of times
questions.explanation: Fuel cells can be refuelled in minutes and only produce water. Batteries take time to recharge and eventually wear out.

questions.question: Give two disadvantages of using hydrogen fuel cells rather than rechargeable batteries to power a car.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: hydrogen is flammable / explosive; hydrogen is a gas that is difficult to store (high-pressure tanks); few hydrogen filling stations; fuel cells are expensive; hydrogen is usually made from fossil fuels or by electrolysis using electricity
questions.explanation: Storing and supplying hydrogen is the main practical problem, and producing it often still relies on fossil fuels.

questions.question: A non-rechargeable cell stops working when one of its reactants is used up. Explain why a fuel cell can keep producing electricity for much longer.
markScheme: 1 mark: the reactants (hydrogen and oxygen) are supplied from outside the cell
1 mark: so they are continuously replaced and do not run out while the supply continues
questions.explanation: In a non-rechargeable cell the reactants are sealed inside. In a fuel cell, fresh fuel and oxygen are fed in continuously.

questions.question: Write the half equation for the reaction at the negative electrode in a hydrogen fuel cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct species (H₂, H⁺ and e⁻) with electrons on the right
1 mark: balanced: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ (or H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻)
questions.explanation: Each hydrogen molecule loses two electrons to form two hydrogen ions. Atoms and charge balance: 0 on the left, 4+ and 4− (total 0) on the right.

questions.question: Write the half equation for the reaction at the positive electrode in a hydrogen fuel cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: O₂, H⁺ and e⁻ on the left and H₂O on the right
1 mark: balanced: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O
questions.explanation: One oxygen molecule gains four electrons and combines with four hydrogen ions to make two water molecules.

questions.question: Explain why the reaction at the negative electrode of a hydrogen fuel cell is described as oxidation.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen (molecules) lose electrons (2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻)
1 mark: loss of electrons is oxidation
questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons (OIL RIG). Hydrogen molecules lose electrons to form H⁺ ions.

questions.question: A newspaper claims: 'Hydrogen fuel cell cars cause no pollution at all.' Evaluate this claim.
acceptedAnswers: manufacture of the car or fuel cell
markScheme: 1 mark: the claim is partly true: the car (fuel cell) only produces water, so no carbon dioxide or pollutants from the exhaust
1 mark: but most hydrogen is made from fossil fuels such as natural gas, or by electrolysis using electricity from fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide
1 mark: conclusion: the claim is not fully correct; pollution may be produced when the hydrogen (or the car) is made, compressed and transported
questions.explanation: An evaluation considers both sides. The exhaust is clean, but the whole life cycle of the fuel may not be.

questions.question: Car makers are developing both battery electric cars (using rechargeable batteries) and hydrogen fuel cell cars. Evaluate the use of hydrogen fuel cells compared with rechargeable batteries for powering cars.
markScheme: Indicative content. Fuel cells: supplied with hydrogen and oxygen from the air; only product is water, so no carbon dioxide at the point of use; refuelled quickly; keep working as long as fuel is supplied, so long range; fewer toxic metal compounds to dispose of; but hydrogen is flammable and is a gas that needs high-pressure storage tanks; few filling stations; expensive; hydrogen often produced from natural gas (fossil fuel) or by electrolysis using electricity, which may come from fossil fuels. Rechargeable batteries: can be charged from mains electricity at home; well-developed technology and charging points widely available; no flammable gas storage; but slow to recharge; limited number of recharge cycles, so eventually need replacing; contain metal compounds that are toxic and must be disposed of or recycled carefully; electricity for charging may come from fossil fuels. Justified conclusion, for example fuel cells better for long-distance vehicles if hydrogen is made using renewable electricity; batteries better for most cars today because charging is more convenient.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a balanced evaluation with advantages and disadvantages of both fuel cells and rechargeable batteries, and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): advantages and disadvantages given for at least one of the two, with some comparison; conclusion may be missing or not justified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple, isolated statements about fuel cells or batteries.
questions.explanation: A top answer compares both technologies point by point (products, refuelling, storage, cost, disposal, how the energy source is produced) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

questions.question: Describe how a hydrogen fuel cell produces electricity. Include the half equations for the reactions at each electrode.
markScheme: Indicative content: hydrogen is supplied to the negative electrode and oxygen (air) to the positive electrode; at the negative electrode hydrogen is oxidised (loses electrons): 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻; the electrons flow through the external circuit from the negative to the positive electrode, which is the electric current; the H⁺ ions move through the electrolyte to the positive electrode; at the positive electrode oxygen is reduced (gains electrons): O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O; overall 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O; water is the only product.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description of the processes at both electrodes with both half equations correct, and the flow of electrons through the external circuit.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct points, for example hydrogen and oxygen react to form water, or one correct half equation.
questions.explanation: The electric current is the flow of electrons released by oxidation of hydrogen at the negative electrode and used in the reduction of oxygen at the positive electrode.
